name: Chitosan

lead: Chitosan is a natural polymer made from chitin in shrimp and crab shells. For appearance it shows up in two forms: an over-the-counter fat-binder supplement sold for a leaner physique, and a carrier polymer in skincare.

In the supplement, the idea is that it binds dietary fat so fewer calories are absorbed. Wikipedia reports that reviews in 2008 and 2016 found no significant effect on weight or cholesterol. In cosmetics, its amine groups become positively charged in acid, letting it form films, gels and nanoparticles that stick to tissue and carry other ingredients, for example improving skin retention of actives such as resveratrol. No human study of chitosan for skin pigmentation was found.

paras: Supplements are taken orally with meals, and chitosan is used as an ingredient in topical and nanoparticle formulations that deliver other actives.
Crustacean-derived chitosan may carry allergenic proteins, according to Grokipedia. The FDA issued a 2015 advisory about exaggerated weight-loss claims by supplement retailers.

angle.text: Sold as a fat binder so fewer calories are absorbed and the physique gets leaner, and used as a carrier polymer in cosmetics. Reviews cited by Wikipedia found no significant weight effect, and no skin-pigment effect has been shown.

lead: Chitosan is a linear polysaccharide made by partially deacetylating chitin, the structural material of crustacean shells, fungal cell walls and insect exoskeletons.[1][2][3] It dissolves in dilute acid and is used in wound care, agriculture, food, water treatment and medicine, with cosmetic delivery systems and weight-loss supplements being the uses most connected to appearance.[1][2]

People use chitosan for their looks in two main ways. In skincare and hair-care research it serves as a film-forming, skin-adhering carrier that can hold actives such as resveratrol against the skin and protect them from light, and its positive charge lets it bind to negatively charged hair and skin surfaces.[1] In the supplement aisle it is sold as a tablet 'fat binder' that proponents say limits dietary fat absorption and so helps with leanness, a claim that has circulated among bodybuilding forum users.[1][4][5][6]

Research on the weight claim is mixed in how it is described. A Cochrane review updated in 2008, covering 15 trials and 1,219 participants, found about 1.7 kg more weight loss than placebo in short-term trials, while noting that trials were often of poor quality and that higher-quality trials showed minimal effects that were unlikely to be clinically significant.[7] Wikipedia cites reviews from 2008 and 2016 finding no significant effect on weight or cholesterol, and records a 2015 US FDA advisory about exaggerated weight-loss claims by supplement retailers.[1] Registered human trials of chitosan for skin pigmentation or other cosmetic outcomes were not found; registered trials concern dental, haemostatic and wound-care uses.[8][9]

paras: Chitosan consists of randomly distributed glucosamine and N-acetylglucosamine units joined by beta-1,4 links; commercial products range from about 60 to 100 percent deacetylation, and the amine groups have a pKa of about 6.3, so the polymer is insoluble in pure water but dissolves in dilute acid and carries positive charge there.[1][2] That charge helps it bind negatively charged surfaces such as mucous membranes and underlies its film-forming, mucoadhesive and antimicrobial behaviour.[1][10][11]

Chitin, its parent material, is described as the second most abundant polysaccharide in nature after cellulose and is extracted commercially from crab, shrimp and lobster shells, which are seafood-industry by-products.[3] Commercial chitosan is usually made by treating this chitin with sodium hydroxide; fungal chitosan is offered as a vegan alternative with more consistent batch quality, according to Grokipedia.[1][2] Molecular weight and degree of deacetylation determine solubility and biological activity.[2]

Chitosan can be chemically modified at its amine and hydroxyl groups. Wikipedia lists phosphorylated, thiolated and quaternized (permanently charged) forms, each designed to change solubility, adhesion or antimicrobial behaviour.[1] Reviews describe tuning chitosan's structure to enhance its biological functions.[2]

Charles Hatchett decalcified crustacean shells in 1799 and found the cartilage-like residue now known as chitin; Charles Rouget treated chitin with alkali in 1859 and obtained a form soluble in dilute acids; and Felix Hoppe-Seyler named it chitosan in 1894.[1] Albert Hofmann determined chitin's structure in 1929.[3] The first chitosan films and fibres were patented around 1930, but cheap petroleum-derived polymers limited uptake, and interest revived in the 1970s, partly because laws restricted dumping of untreated shellfish waste.[1]

Chitosan was first registered as an active ingredient in 1986, initially in agriculture as a plant-defence elicitor, and the US EPA approved elicitor status for a 0.25 percent chitosan product in 2008.[1] Chitosan haemostatic dressings were approved in the United States from 2003, with gauzes and granules following in 2006.[1] In 2000 a temperature-sensitive chitosan hydrogel that is liquid at room temperature and gels at body temperature was described, opening the way to injectable carriers.[1] Researchers have since explored it as a carrier in hydrogels and nanoparticles for drugs and cosmetic actives.[12][13][14]

Chitosan is widely studied as a vehicle for delivering drugs and cosmetic actives through hydrogels, nanoparticles and emulsions.[12][13][14] In a laboratory study with porcine skin, chitosan/gum Arabic Pickering emulsions raised retention of resveratrol and improved its photostability; a related study reported that nanocarriers enhanced transdermal delivery of resveratrol. Wikipedia also notes a 2025 paper on chitosan conjugates as ingredients in rinse-off hair conditioners.[1]

The appearance rationale is that a positively charged film adheres to skin and hair and can hold an active in place, protect it from degradation and slow its release, so the active has more time at the surface.[10]

Chitosan binds fibrinogen and promotes platelet adhesion, and it is used in haemostatic dressings such as chitosan fibre and gauze products and in hydrogel dressings for burns and chronic wounds.[1][15][16] Reviews describe antimicrobial properties and applications ranging from dental materials to vaccine delivery.[17][9][18][19] Smoother, faster wound healing is relevant to how a scar looks, although the studies cited here do not measure cosmetic scar outcomes.

Chitosan is sold in tablet form as a fat binder, on the theory that its positive charge attracts negatively charged dietary fats and bile acids in the gut so that they pass through unabsorbed.[1] A 2023 network meta-analysis of 111 randomised trials ranked many nutraceuticals for weight loss in adults with overweight or obesity.[20] Two 2025 randomised trials of chitosan products in overweight adults have been published: one of 60 Thai women taking chitosan oligosaccharide for 60 days and one of 60 adults combining chitosan with moderate exercise for 12 weeks.[7]

Outside medicine, chitosan is used as a seed treatment and biopesticide, a flocculant in water filtration, a fining agent for wine and beer, and in food packaging films.[1] Because commercial sources are shellfish by-products, production overlaps with the seafood industry.[3]

For topical delivery, the research consists of laboratory and animal work: porcine skin experiments and nanoparticle studies report improved retention and stability of actives.[12] Human trials of cosmetic outcomes were not found.

For weight, results depend on which analysis is read. The 2008 Cochrane review of 15 trials (1,219 participants) reported a weighted mean difference of -1.7 kg versus placebo and a 0.2 mmol/L fall in total cholesterol, with no clear differences in adverse events or faecal fat excretion, and its authors noted that higher-quality trials showed minimal effects.[7] Reviews cited by Wikipedia from 2008 and 2016 concluded that any effect on body weight or cholesterol is of low clinical importance.[1]

The 2025 trial in Thai women (chitosan oligosaccharide at two dose levels versus placebo for 60 days) found no significant between-group lipid differences by intention to treat, though HDL rose within the lower-dose group.[7] The 2025 exercise trial reported greater reductions in body weight and waist circumference with chitosan plus exercise than with exercise alone or control over 12 weeks, with no significant difference in adverse events.[7]

In T Nation discussions, a coach answering a reader called chitosan something that 'looks good on paper' but 'doesn't do much' in practice, while other users have described using it during diet phases or for creatinine.[21][22]

Grokipedia notes that chitosan from crustacean sources can carry allergenic proteins and variable purity because of environmental contaminants, while the FDA has classified chitosan as generally recognised as safe.[2] The Cochrane review found no clear differences in adverse events between chitosan and placebo.[7] A systematic review of food and supplement interactions with warfarin lists dietary supplements among agents reported to interact with the anticoagulant, so clinicians commonly ask about supplements in people taking it.[23] Wikipedia notes the FDA has not approved chitosan for drug delivery.[1]

Chitosan was one of several fat-loss supplements promoted in bodybuilding magazines and forums in earlier decades; T Nation users have listed it alongside other products that were 'the next big thing' for getting lean.[5][6] In a 2005 forum thread about the anabolic diet, a user asked whether chitosan could count as fibre since it is relatively cheap.[24]

A 2015 US FDA advisory about exaggerated weight-loss claims by supplement retailers is recorded by Wikipedia.[1] In agriculture the material is registered as a basic substance and elicitor in the EU, UK and US.[1] In research it is an active area: reviews cover chitosan vaccine delivery, dentistry, wound hydrogels and nanoparticles against infections.[9][18][19]

No studies found examining chitosan for skin pigmentation or other cosmetic appearance outcomes. Weight-related human research includes the Cochrane review of 15 trials and two 2025 randomised trials in overweight adults.[7][7] Registered trials in other areas include chitosan powder in a cervical excision procedure (130 participants), chitosan mouthwash for dental black stains in children (17 participants, crossover) and a chewing gum study in dialysis patients (15 participants).[8][9][25] A 2025 randomised trial studied carboxymethyl-chitosan in knee osteoarthritis over twelve months.[26]
